    Evaluate a Pose Estimation Model with COCO Keypoint mAP¶

    Pose models are scored on COCO with keypoint mAP. Instead of box IoU, a prediction is matched to a person by Object Keypoint Similarity (OKS): a 0 to 1 score of how close each predicted keypoint lands to the labelled one, relative to the person's size and to how precisely that keypoint can be placed. This cookbook runs RF-DETR Keypoint on a slice of COCO val2017 and scores it with KeyPointMeanAveragePrecision. Along the way it shows two mistakes that can change the score without raising an error: scoring only high-confidence predictions, and mismatched class ids.

    A GPU runtime is recommended (Runtime → Change runtime type). The stored outputs were produced on a Mac with Apple silicon (MPS), and the notebook has not been run on Colab. CPU should also work, but it is untested here and the RF-DETR Keypoint checkpoint is large, so 200 images take noticeably longer.

    Install required packages¶

    • supervision[metrics]: keypoint containers, annotators and KeyPointMeanAveragePrecision. Version 0.31.7 or newer: in earlier versions sv.KeyPoints.empty() holds None fields, which breaks the confidence filter used below on frames without poses. The metrics extra adds pandas for to_pandas.
    • rfdetr: provides RFDETRKeypointPreview, a COCO-pretrained 17-keypoint person model. It is a preview release whose API and weights may change, so the version is pinned.
    In [ ]:

    Load COCO keypoint annotations¶

    We download the official COCO 2017 annotations (about 241 MB) and extract only person_keypoints_val2017.json. To keep the run short, we sample 200 of the 2,693 val2017 images that contain at least one annotated person, with a fixed seed, so every run scores the same images. Because images without people are left out and the slice is small, the score below is a worked example, not a replacement for the full COCO benchmark. The seed fixes only the image sample: model outputs are not seeded, so scores can differ slightly on other devices and library versions. The numbers below come from a Mac with Apple silicon (MPS).

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    ANNOTATIONS_URL = "http://images.cocodataset.org/annotations/annotations_trainval2017.zip"
# the host's https certificate does not match its name, so verify the plain-http download instead
ANNOTATIONS_SHA256 = "113a836d90195ee1f884e704da6304dfaaecff1f023f49b6ca93c4aaae470268"
ANNOTATIONS_FILE = Path("person_keypoints_val2017.json")

if not ANNOTATIONS_FILE.exists():
    archive_path, _ = urllib.request.urlretrieve(ANNOTATIONS_URL)  # temporary file
    try:
        if hashlib.sha256(Path(archive_path).read_bytes()).hexdigest() != ANNOTATIONS_SHA256:
            raise ValueError("the downloaded COCO annotations do not match the expected SHA-256")
        with zipfile.ZipFile(archive_path) as archive:
            # write under a temporary name so an interrupted run never leaves a broken JSON file
            partial = ANNOTATIONS_FILE.with_suffix(".part")
            partial.write_bytes(archive.read(f"annotations/{ANNOTATIONS_FILE}"))
            partial.rename(ANNOTATIONS_FILE)
    finally:
        Path(archive_path).unlink()

coco = json.loads(ANNOTATIONS_FILE.read_text())
images = {image["id"]: image for image in coco["images"]}
annotations = {}
for annotation in coco["annotations"]:
    annotations.setdefault(annotation["image_id"], []).append(annotation)

image_ids = sorted(random.Random(0).sample(sorted(annotations), 200))
people = [a for i in image_ids for a in annotations[i]]
print(f"{len(image_ids)} images, {len(people)} person annotations, "
      f"{sum(a['num_keypoints'] == 0 for a in people)} of them without labelled keypoints")

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    IMAGE_DIR = Path("images")
IMAGE_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
IMAGE_URL_PREFIX = "http://images.cocodataset.org/"


def download(image_id: int) -> None:
    """Download one COCO image into ``IMAGE_DIR``, refusing any other destination or host."""
    image = images[image_id]
    path = IMAGE_DIR / Path(image["file_name"]).name  # keep only the file name from the annotation
    inside_image_dir = path.resolve().parent == IMAGE_DIR.resolve()
    if not inside_image_dir or not image["coco_url"].startswith(IMAGE_URL_PREFIX):
        raise ValueError(f"unexpected image location for {image['file_name']}")
    if not path.exists():
        # download under a temporary name so an interrupted run never leaves a broken image
        partial = path.with_suffix(".part")
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(image["coco_url"], partial)
        partial.rename(path)


with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16) as pool:
    list(pool.map(download, image_ids))
    IMAGE_DIR = Path("images") IMAGE_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True) IMAGE_URL_PREFIX = "http://images.cocodataset.org/" def download(image_id: int) -> None: """Download one COCO image into ``IMAGE_DIR``, refusing any other destination or host.""" image = images[image_id] path = IMAGE_DIR / Path(image["file_name"]).name # keep only the file name from the annotation inside_image_dir = path.resolve().parent == IMAGE_DIR.resolve() if not inside_image_dir or not image["coco_url"].startswith(IMAGE_URL_PREFIX): raise ValueError(f"unexpected image location for {image['file_name']}") if not path.exists(): # download under a temporary name so an interrupted run never leaves a broken image partial = path.with_suffix(".part") urllib.request.urlretrieve(image["coco_url"], partial) partial.rename(path) with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16) as pool: list(pool.map(download, image_ids))

    Turn COCO annotations into sv.KeyPoints¶

    Each COCO person carries 17 (x, y, v) keypoints. We keep v > 0 as visible, since COCO evaluation counts occluded (v=1) and visible (v=2) points alike. Three extra fields bring the score in line with pycocotools:

    • data["area"]: the annotated area, which scales OKS and sets the size buckets (medium: an area of 32² to 96² pixels, large: above 96²).
    • data["iscrowd"]: crowd annotations, where one label covers a group of people. They act as ignore regions: predictions that match them are not counted as false positives.
    • data["xyxy"]: the person box. Many COCO people have no labelled keypoints (counted above). With a box, such a person is an ignore region, as in pycocotools. Without one it is dropped, and predictions on it count as false positives.

    See the pose estimation section of the metric docs for the full rules.

    The class id is set to 1 because the COCO-pretrained RF-DETR model reports people with the COCO category id 1, not 0. Predictions and targets are grouped by class, so the two must agree.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    # COCO person keypoints: 17 points per person, one class (category id 1)
def coco_to_keypoints(person_annotations: list[dict]) -> sv.KeyPoints:
    keypoints = np.array([a["keypoints"] for a in person_annotations], dtype=np.float32)
    keypoints = keypoints.reshape(-1, 17, 3)
    boxes = np.array([a["bbox"] for a in person_annotations], dtype=np.float32)
    return sv.KeyPoints(
        xy=keypoints[..., :2],
        visible=keypoints[..., 2] > 0,
        class_id=np.ones(len(keypoints), dtype=int),  # must match the model's class id
        data={
            # float64: float32 rounding can put an area near 32² or 96² into two size buckets
            "area": np.array([a["area"] for a in person_annotations], dtype=np.float64),
            "iscrowd": np.array([a["iscrowd"] for a in person_annotations], dtype=bool),
            "xyxy": sv.xywh_to_xyxy(boxes),  # COCO boxes are xywh
        },
    )


targets = [coco_to_keypoints(annotations[image_id]) for image_id in image_ids]
    # COCO person keypoints: 17 points per person, one class (category id 1) def coco_to_keypoints(person_annotations: list[dict]) -> sv.KeyPoints: keypoints = np.array([a["keypoints"] for a in person_annotations], dtype=np.float32) keypoints = keypoints.reshape(-1, 17, 3) boxes = np.array([a["bbox"] for a in person_annotations], dtype=np.float32) return sv.KeyPoints( xy=keypoints[..., :2], visible=keypoints[..., 2] > 0, class_id=np.ones(len(keypoints), dtype=int), # must match the model's class id data={ # float64: float32 rounding can put an area near 32² or 96² into two size buckets "area": np.array([a["area"] for a in person_annotations], dtype=np.float64), "iscrowd": np.array([a["iscrowd"] for a in person_annotations], dtype=bool), "xyxy": sv.xywh_to_xyxy(boxes), # COCO boxes are xywh }, ) targets = [coco_to_keypoints(annotations[image_id]) for image_id in image_ids]

    Run RF-DETR Keypoint¶

    model.predict returns an sv.KeyPoints with per-person detection_confidence, per-point keypoint_confidence and the person box in data["xyxy"]. Its threshold drops low-scoring people, and the default 0.5 suits visualization. For mAP we keep almost everything (0.01): the metric ranks predictions by detection_confidence and needs the low-confidence tail to trace the full precision-recall curve. That leaves many candidates per image, but the metric uses only the 20 highest-scoring ones, as COCO does.

    When you run it, loading the model prints a few rf-detr INFO and WARNING lines about weights and classes; they are expected for this preview checkpoint.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    model = RFDETRKeypointPreview()


def load_image(image_id: int) -> np.ndarray:
    return np.array(Image.open(IMAGE_DIR / images[image_id]["file_name"]).convert("RGB"))


predictions = [model.predict(load_image(image_id), threshold=0.01) for image_id in image_ids]
print(f"{sum(len(p) for p in predictions)} predicted people")
    model = RFDETRKeypointPreview() def load_image(image_id: int) -> np.ndarray: return np.array(Image.open(IMAGE_DIR / images[image_id]["file_name"]).convert("RGB")) predictions = [model.predict(load_image(image_id), threshold=0.01) for image_id in image_ids] print(f"{sum(len(p) for p in predictions)} predicted people")
    17177 predicted people

    Here are two of the images, with the ground truth on the left and the confident predictions (detection_confidence > 0.5) on the right. We show the two images with the most people who have at least 12 labelled keypoints, so there are near-complete skeletons to compare:

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    edge_annotator = sv.EdgeAnnotator(color=sv.Color.GREEN, thickness=3)
vertex_annotator = sv.VertexAnnotator(color=sv.Color.RED, radius=4)

# the two images with the most nearly complete skeletons
showcase = sorted(range(len(image_ids)), key=lambda i: -(targets[i].visible.sum(axis=1) >= 12).sum())[:2]

for index in showcase:
    # annotators and plot_images_grid accept PIL images, so no BGR channel handling is needed
    image = Image.fromarray(load_image(image_ids[index]))
    confident = predictions[index][predictions[index].detection_confidence > 0.5]
    labelled = targets[index][targets[index].visible.any(axis=1)]
    panels = []
    for key_points in (labelled, confident):
        panel = edge_annotator.annotate(image.copy(), key_points)
        panels.append(vertex_annotator.annotate(panel, key_points))
    titles = [f"ground truth: {len(labelled)} people", f"RF-DETR, confidence > 0.5: {len(confident)} people"]
    sv.plot_images_grid(panels, grid_size=(1, 2), titles=titles, size=(12, 5))
    edge_annotator = sv.EdgeAnnotator(color=sv.Color.GREEN, thickness=3) vertex_annotator = sv.VertexAnnotator(color=sv.Color.RED, radius=4) # the two images with the most nearly complete skeletons showcase = sorted(range(len(image_ids)), key=lambda i: -(targets[i].visible.sum(axis=1) >= 12).sum())[:2] for index in showcase: # annotators and plot_images_grid accept PIL images, so no BGR channel handling is needed image = Image.fromarray(load_image(image_ids[index])) confident = predictions[index][predictions[index].detection_confidence > 0.5] labelled = targets[index][targets[index].visible.any(axis=1)] panels = [] for key_points in (labelled, confident): panel = edge_annotator.annotate(image.copy(), key_points) panels.append(vertex_annotator.annotate(panel, key_points)) titles = [f"ground truth: {len(labelled)} people", f"RF-DETR, confidence > 0.5: {len(confident)} people"] sv.plot_images_grid(panels, grid_size=(1, 2), titles=titles, size=(12, 5))

    Compute keypoint mAP¶

    KeyPointMeanAveragePrecision follows COCO keypoint evaluation: OKS thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95, up to 20 predictions per image, and medium and large buckets only, since COCO keypoint labels cover only people of at least 32² pixels. With 17 keypoints it uses the COCO sigmas, the per-keypoint tolerances in OKS, by default.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    result = KeyPointMeanAveragePrecision().update(predictions, targets).compute()
print(result)
    result = KeyPointMeanAveragePrecision().update(predictions, targets).compute() print(result)

Average Precision (AP) @[ OKS=0.75      | area=   all | maxDets= 20 ] = 0.800
Average Precision (AP) @[ OKS=0.50:0.95 | area=medium | maxDets= 20 ] = 0.664
Average Precision (AP) @[ OKS=0.50:0.95 | area= large | maxDets= 20 ] = 0.820

    Large people score higher than medium ones (about 0.82 against 0.66 mAP50:95), because OKS tolerates fewer pixels of error on a small body. The same scores are in the table below.

    Two mistakes that change the score silently¶

    Neither mistake below raises a warning: the first returns a lower but plausible score, the second returns 0 for a model that works. Since the predictions are already computed, we can show each one without running the model again.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    def keypoint_map(predictions: list[sv.KeyPoints], targets: list[sv.KeyPoints]) -> float:
    return KeyPointMeanAveragePrecision().update(predictions, targets).compute().map50_95


# 1. Scoring only the predictions that survive the display threshold
displayed = [p[p.detection_confidence > 0.5] for p in predictions]
print(f"threshold 0.01: mAP50-95 = {result.map50_95:.3f}")
print(f"threshold 0.5:  mAP50-95 = {keypoint_map(displayed, targets):.3f}")

# 2. Targets labelled with class 0 while the model reports COCO id 1
shifted = [dataclasses.replace(t, class_id=np.zeros_like(t.class_id)) for t in targets]
print(f"class ids 1 vs 0: mAP50-95 = {keypoint_map(predictions, shifted):.3f}")
    def keypoint_map(predictions: list[sv.KeyPoints], targets: list[sv.KeyPoints]) -> float: return KeyPointMeanAveragePrecision().update(predictions, targets).compute().map50_95 # 1. Scoring only the predictions that survive the display threshold displayed = [p[p.detection_confidence > 0.5] for p in predictions] print(f"threshold 0.01: mAP50-95 = {result.map50_95:.3f}") print(f"threshold 0.5: mAP50-95 = {keypoint_map(displayed, targets):.3f}") # 2. Targets labelled with class 0 while the model reports COCO id 1 shifted = [dataclasses.replace(t, class_id=np.zeros_like(t.class_id)) for t in targets] print(f"class ids 1 vs 0: mAP50-95 = {keypoint_map(predictions, shifted):.3f}")
    threshold 0.01: mAP50-95 = 0.729
threshold 0.5:  mAP50-95 = 0.658
class ids 1 vs 0: mAP50-95 = 0.000

    If your labels and model disagree on ids, remap one side, or pass class_agnostic=True to KeyPointMeanAveragePrecision when there is a single class.

    Using your own data¶

    • A different skeleton. For anything other than the 17 COCO keypoints, pass one OKS sigma per keypoint: KeyPointMeanAveragePrecision(sigmas=...). Predictions and targets must also list keypoints in the same order.
    • Images without people. Pass sv.KeyPoints.empty() as the target, so predictions on those images still count as false positives (coco_to_keypoints above expects at least one person). This cookbook samples only images with people, which is one reason its score differs from the full benchmark.
    • No annotated area. Without data["area"] the box spanning a target's visible keypoints is used, so scores may differ from COCO's.
    • Object size of predictions. A prediction falls into the medium or large bucket by its box in data["xyxy"] when present, otherwise by the box spanning its keypoints. This matches pycocotools with and without a result bbox.
    • Other models. Any source that can be turned into sv.KeyPoints works the same way, for example sv.KeyPoints.from_ultralytics(...) for YOLO pose models. Check which class ids each source uses.

    Conclusion¶

    Keypoint mAP needs only two lists of sv.KeyPoints, but COCO-comparable numbers depend on keeping low-confidence predictions, matching class ids, and passing the annotated area, crowd flags and boxes. For the complete rules, see the KeyPointMeanAveragePrecision docs; for drawing skeletons, see the keypoint annotators.
